learning_goal: Identify each of the four chambers in a cut heart by its own wall markings, name what enters and leaves it, and explain why the left ventricle is thick and the right is thin.

terms: valve of the inferior vena cava

structures.label: Right atrium
structures.narration: Receives all the deoxygenated blood of the body — superior vena cava above, inferior vena cava below, coronary sinus between them. It forms the whole right border of the heart.

structures.label: Right ventricle
structures.narration: Forms most of the front of the heart, so it is the chamber a knife or a needle reaches first. Its wall is about 3 to 5 mm thick and it is crescent-shaped in cross-section, wrapped round the left ventricle.

structures.label: Left atrium
structures.narration: The most posterior chamber, taking four pulmonary veins. It lies directly in front of the oesophagus, which is why an enlarged left atrium shows on a barium swallow and why the echo probe goes down the gullet.

structures.label: Left ventricle
structures.narration: Forms the apex and the left border. Its wall is three times the thickness of the right — 8 to 12 mm — and it is circular in section, because it pumps against the whole body's resistance rather than the lungs' alone.

structures.label: Crista terminalis
structures.narration: A vertical muscular ridge dividing the atrium into a smooth posterior part from the sinus venosus and a rough anterior part from the true atrium. The SA node sits at its upper end.

structures.label: Pectinate muscles & right auricle
structures.narration: Parallel muscle ridges like the teeth of a comb, in front of the crista and inside the auricle. The same ridges line the left auricle, and it is there — not here — that blood stagnates in atrial fibrillation and the clot of a cardioembolic stroke forms. A clot on this side goes to the lungs, not the brain.

structures.label: Fossa ovalis
structures.narration: A shallow oval dip on the septal wall — the closed remnant of the foramen ovale, with the limbus as its raised upper rim. It fails to seal in about a quarter of adults, which is how a venous clot can cross to the systemic side.

structures.label: Openings: SVC, IVC & coronary sinus
terms: valve of the inferior vena cava
structures.narration: Three inlets and no valves worth the name. The superior cava enters above with nothing guarding it, the inferior cava below behind a rudimentary Eustachian valve, and the coronary sinus between the inferior cava and the tricuspid opening.

structures.label: Trabeculae carneae
structures.narration: Irregular muscular ridges lining both ventricles. They are coarse in the right ventricle and finer in the left, so a cut chamber can be told apart by feel alone.

structures.label: Moderator band
structures.narration: A muscular strut crossing from the septum to the anterior papillary muscle — found only in the right ventricle. It carries the right bundle branch, so the apex is activated at the same time as the base.

structures.label: Papillary muscles & chordae tendineae
structures.narration: Three in the right ventricle, two in the left. They tighten as the ventricle contracts and hold the cusps down, so the valve stays flat instead of blowing back into the atrium.

structures.label: Infundibulum (conus arteriosus)
structures.narration: The smooth funnel leading out of the right ventricle to the pulmonary valve. Narrowing here is the obstruction in tetralogy of Fallot.

structures.label: Aortic vestibule
structures.narration: The smooth-walled outflow of the left ventricle below the aortic valve. Unlike the right, its inflow and outflow lie side by side, separated only by the anterior cusp of the mitral valve.

structures.label: Interatrial septum
structures.narration: The thin wall between the atria, carrying the fossa ovalis. A hole here shunts left to right and gives fixed splitting of the second heart sound.

structures.label: Interventricular septum — muscular part
structures.narration: Thick, muscular, and bulging into the right ventricle because the left side's pressure is higher. It behaves as part of the left ventricle.

structures.label: Interventricular septum — membranous part
structures.narration: A small fibrous patch at the top, where the septum meets the valves. It is the last part to close in the fetus and the commonest site of a ventricular septal defect — a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge.

structures.label: Tricuspid valve
structures.narration: The door from right atrium to right ventricle.

structures.label: Mitral valve
structures.narration: The door from left atrium to left ventricle.

structures.label: Pulmonary valve
structures.narration: The exit from the right ventricle.

structures.label: Aortic valve
structures.narration: The exit from the left ventricle, with the coronary arteries opening just above two of its cusps.

structures.label: Superior & inferior vena cava
structures.narration: Bring the body's blood into the right atrium.

structures.label: Pulmonary veins
structures.narration: Four of them, entering the back of the left atrium.

structures.label: Pulmonary trunk & aorta
structures.narration: The two exits, crossing each other as they leave — the pulmonary trunk starts in front and passes to the left, the aorta starts behind it.

views.title: Four chambers, two pumps
views.narration: Two atria above, two ventricles below, and a septum keeping the right side from the left. The right side is a low-pressure pump sending blood a short way to the lungs; the left is a high-pressure pump sending it everywhere else. Almost every difference between the chambers comes from that one fact.

views.title: Open the right atrium
views.narration: Cut it open and one ridge explains the whole chamber. In front of the crista terminalis the wall is rough with pectinate muscles — that part came from the embryonic atrium. Behind it the wall is smooth — that part is absorbed vena cava. On the septal wall sits the fossa ovalis, and between the inferior cava and the tricuspid opening is the mouth of the coronary sinus.

views.title: Open the right ventricle
views.narration: The inflow is rough with coarse trabeculae; the outflow is a smooth funnel, the infundibulum, leading up to the pulmonary valve. Crossing the cavity is the moderator band, which no other chamber has — it carries the right bundle branch from the septum to the anterior papillary muscle. Find the moderator band and you have found the right ventricle.

views.title: Open the left side
views.narration: The left atrium is smooth almost everywhere, with pectinate muscle only in its auricle, and takes four pulmonary veins at the back. The left ventricle has fine trabeculae, two large papillary muscles, and a smooth aortic vestibule beside its inlet. Compare the two ventricles in section: the left is a thick circle, the right a thin crescent draped over it. A right ventricle that looks like the left has been pumping against pulmonary hypertension.

views.title: The septa and where they leak
views.narration: The interatrial septum is thin and carries the fossa ovalis. The interventricular septum is mostly thick muscle that belongs functionally to the left ventricle, with a small membranous patch at the top. That patch is the last part to close before birth and the commonest place a hole is left — a loud pansystolic murmur at the left sternal edge, and the smaller the hole the louder the noise.

views.title: Follow one red cell
views.narration: Vena cava to right atrium, through the tricuspid to the right ventricle, up the infundibulum and out the pulmonary valve to the lungs. Back through four pulmonary veins to the left atrium, through the mitral valve to the left ventricle, up the vestibule and out the aortic valve to the body. Say the order out loud until the chamber and its door come as one pair.

views.title: Tell them apart in the pot
views.narration: The spotter asks which chamber this is. Crista terminalis, pectinate muscles reaching well beyond the auricle, a fossa ovalis and the mouth of the coronary sinus: right atrium. Smooth walls, four veins entering behind, pectinate muscle only in the auricle: left atrium. A moderator band, coarse trabeculae, three papillary muscles and a thin crescentic wall: right ventricle. Thick circular wall, two papillary muscles, fine trabeculae and the apex: left ventricle.

gaps: Routed to its deferred diagram mode, not to 3D. The catalog holds no chamber at all: searching all 934 entries for atrium, ventricle, chamber and septum returns the four ventricles of the BRAIN, the septum pellucidum, the papillary muscles and the wall of heart, and nothing cardiac that is a chamber. The heart scene gross__heart-pericardium__heart deliberately does not claim to cover this structure for that reason, and authoring a second 3D scene from the same valves and papillary muscles would have repeated it without teaching a chamber.

The chambers ARE in the full BodyParts3D archive and this gap is closable without rewriting the curriculum: right atrium FMA7096, left atrium FMA7097, right ventricle FMA7098, left ventricle FMA7101, aortic valve FMA7236, interventricular septum FMA7133. Run tools/ingest-full-archive.mjs --fetch on those ids, then re-author this scene as 3d_anatomy — the structure list, the beats and the narration all survive the move.

Status is 'planned', not 'ready'. The scene is fully authored — twenty-three regions, seven beats, ops and narration — but no artwork has been drawn for the SVG engine, so nothing renders today. Promote it to 'ready' once a four-chamber cut drawing exists with the labelled regions this scene names, or once the ingest above lets it become a 3D scene.

The valves and great vessels are authored as context regions here even though six of them DO exist in the catalog (tricuspid FMA7234, mitral FMA7235, pulmonary FMA7246, and the caval, pulmonary and aortic vessels). They are context because the valves are taught in full by the heart scene; this scene borrows them only as the doors between chambers. The aortic valve is the one door with no model in either set.

Beat 6 traces concept:blood through thirteen waypoints, several of which are the chambers themselves rather than a lumen. That is deliberate: the point of the beat is the ORDER, and a student who can say the order can answer the flow question in any form the exam asks it.

Audit 2026-08-29: beat 6's path steps straight from pulm_valve to pulm_veins_in, and its narration says 'out the pulmonary valve to the lungs'. The lungs, the pulmonary trunk's division and the pulmonary capillary bed are NOT drawn in this scene — the leg of the circuit between those two waypoints is described, not shown. Left as-is because the beat is explicitly about chamber order, but the illustrator should not draw a vessel joining those two points, and a student should not be asked to trace it.

Wall thicknesses are given as the standard 3-5 mm right and 8-12 mm left. Chamber volumes, the conduction system's course through the septum, and the fibrous skeleton are not drawn — the conduction system has its own curriculum entry and its own scene to come.
